content: Cefaclor is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for the treatment of various infections, including otitis media, lower respiratory tract infections, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, urinary tract infections, and skin structure infections. Common adverse reactions associated with its use include diarrhea, nervousness, insomnia, confusion, hypertonia, dizziness, asthenia, edema, dyspnea, paresthesias, syncope, and hypotension. Adult Indications and Dosage Cefaclor is indicated for the treatment of infections caused by susceptible strains of specific microorganisms. These include: Otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, staphylococci, and Streptococcus pyogenes. Note that β-lactamase-negative, ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR) strains of Haemophilus influenzae should be considered resistant to cefaclor despite apparent in vitro susceptibility. Lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus pyogenes. The same resistance note applies to BLNAR strains of Haemophilus influenzae. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Penicillin is typically the drug of choice for treating and preventing streptococcal infections, including rheumatic fever prophylaxis. While cefaclor is effective in eradicating streptococci from the nasopharynx, there is insufficient data to confirm its efficacy in preventing rheumatic fever. Skin and skin structure infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of cefaclor, it should only be used to treat or prevent infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide therapy selection. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy. The usual adult dosage is 250 mg every 8 hours. For more severe infections, such as pneumonia, or infections caused by less susceptible organisms, the dose may be doubled. Cefaclor can be administered in the presence of impaired renal function, and dosage adjustments are generally not required. For β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, cefaclor should be administered for at least 10 days. Pediatric Indications and Dosage Cefaclor is also indicated for pediatric patients for the treatment of infections caused by susceptible strains of specific microorganisms, including: Otitis media caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, staphylococci, and Streptococcus pyogenes. The same resistance note applies to BLNAR strains of Haemophilus influenzae. Lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus pyogenes. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. Penicillin remains the usual drug of choice for treating and preventing streptococcal infections, including rheumatic fever prophylaxis. The recommended daily dosage for pediatric patients is 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 hours. For more serious infections, otitis media, or infections caused by less susceptible organisms, 40 mg/kg/day is recommended, with a maximum dosage of 1 g/day. Cefaclor can be administered in the presence of impaired renal function, and dosage adjustments are generally not required. For β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, cefaclor should be administered for at least 10 days. Contraindications Cefaclor is contraindicated in patients with a known allergy to cephalosporin antibiotics. Warnings Before initiating therapy with cefaclor, a thorough inquiry should be made to determine whether the patient has had previous hypersensitivity reactions to cefaclor, cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-hypersensitivity among β-lactam antibiotics has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue the drug immediately. Serious acute hypersensitivity reactions may require treatment with epinephrine and other emergency measures, including oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management as clinically indicated. Antibiotics, including cefaclor, should be used cautiously in patients with a history of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefaclor, and may range in severity from mild to life-threatening. It is important to consider this diagnosis in patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic administration. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions to cefaclor include: Hypersensitivity reactions: These may range from mild skin eruptions to severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and anaphylaxis. Serum sickness-like reactions have also been reported, characterized by erythema multiforme, rash, arthritis/arthralgia, and fever. These reactions are more common during or after a second course of therapy. Gastrointestinal effects: Diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and epigastric distress have been reported. Pseudomembranous colitis symptoms may occur during or after antibiotic treatment. Hepatic effects: Transient elevations in AST, ALT, or alkaline phosphatase values have been observed. Hematologic effects: Transient lymphocytosis, leukopenia, and, rarely, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis, and reversible neutropenia have been reported. Renal effects: Slight elevations in BUN or serum creatinine and abnormal urinalysis have been reported rarely. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Cefaclor is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies have not shown harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Cefaclor should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Nursing mothers: Small amounts of cefaclor have been detected in breast milk. The effect on nursing infants is unknown, and caution should be exercised when administering cefaclor to nursing women. Pediatric use: Safety and effectiveness in infants less than 1 month of age have not been established. Elderly patients: No overall differences in safety or effectiveness have been observed between elderly and younger patients. However, elderly patients are more likely to have decreased renal function, which may increase the risk of toxic reactions. Administration and Monitoring Cefaclor is administered orally. Monitoring information is limited in the drug label. Overdosage Symptoms of cefaclor overdose may include nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, and diarrhea. The severity of these symptoms is dose-related. Treatment should focus on supportive measures, including maintaining airway patency, ventilation, and perfusion. Activated charcoal may be considered to reduce drug absorption. Forced diuresis, peritoneal dialysis, hemodialysis, or charcoal hemoperfusion have not been established as beneficial for cefaclor overdose. Pharmacology Cefaclor is a semisynthetic cephalosporin antibiotic for oral administration. It is chemically designated as 3-chloro-7-D-(2-phenylglycinamido)-3-cephem-4-carboxylic acid monohydrate. Its mechanism of action and pharmacokinetics are not well-detailed in the drug label. Storage Cefaclor capsules should be stored at 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F). Patient Counseling Information Patients should be advised that cefaclor is only effective against bacterial infections and should not be used to treat viral infections such as the common cold. It is important to complete the full course of therapy as prescribed to prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria. Skipping doses or not completing the therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the treatment and increase the likelihood of resistance.
